result: The truncated construct Slc26a9T (lacking IVS and CT regions) exhibits greater surface expression, can be purified to homogeneity as a dimer, and retains robust Cl- transport activity that can be inhibited by DIDS. The IVS region appears responsible for intracellular retention of full-length Slc26a9, and the purified protein does not require cellular factors for activity.
evaluation: Claims C27-C32 are well-supported by fluorescence microscopy (C27), comparison of truncation constructs (C28), size-exclusion chromatography (C29), and fluorometric transport assays (C30-C31). The inference that Slc26a9T does not require cellular factors (C32) is directly supported by observing activity in reconstituted proteoliposomes. The data consistently demonstrate that the truncation strategy successfully produced a functional, well-behaved protein suitable for structural and functional studies.

result: Slc26a9T exhibits constitutively active, anion-selective currents with linear I-V relationships in both whole-cell and inside-out patch configurations. Currents are at least 4-fold larger than full-length Slc26a9, reverse at the Cl- Nernst potential (indicating Cl- is the only transported charge), and show saturation at high Cl- concentrations with a Km of 30 mM. No single-channel transitions were observed.
evaluation: Claims C33-C39 are strongly supported by comprehensive electrophysiology data from whole-cell and inside-out patch-clamp recordings. The reversal potential measurements under various ionic gradients (C37) directly support the conclusion that Cl- is the only transported charge (C38). The Km determination (C39) is based on conductance-concentration relationships. The negative result regarding single-channel transitions (C36) contrasts with one previous study but is clearly stated as an observation from the current experiments.

result: Slc26a9T displays a lyotropic permeability sequence (SCN->I->Br->NO3->Cl-) but negligible permeability for F-, HCO3-, and SO42-. The conductivity sequence (Cl->Br->NO3-~SCN->I-) deviates from the permeability sequence, with Cl- being considerably more conductive than other anions. This pattern suggests Slc26a9 has evolved as an efficient uncoupled Cl- transporter, with lyotropic anions facing lower dehydration barriers but deeper energy wells that decrease turnover.
evaluation: Claims C41-C51 are well-supported by systematic bi-ionic substitution experiments and conductance measurements. The permeability sequence (C41) and negligible permeabilities for certain anions (C42) are directly measured. The comparison to previous studies (C43-C45) appropriately contextualizes the findings. The mechanistic interpretations about energy barriers and wells (C48-C49) are reasonable inferences from the permeability and conductance data. The conclusion that Slc26a9 is an efficient Cl- transporter (C51) is supported by the kinetic parameters.

result: The structure of Slc26a9T was determined by cryo-EM at 3.96 Å resolution in detergent and at 7.77 Å resolution in lipid nanodiscs. Both datasets show similar overall organization of subunits and oligomeric arrangement, though the nanodisc structure reveals localized rigid-body movements indicative of a different functional conformation.
evaluation: Claims C52-C55 are supported by the cryo-EM data collection and processing described in the methods and results. The resolutions are appropriate for the conclusions drawn, with the detergent structure at near-atomic resolution allowing detailed model building, and the lower-resolution nanodisc structure sufficient to observe conformational differences. The comparison between the two structures (C54-C55) is directly observable from the structural data and provides important validation that the detergent environment did not introduce major artifacts.

result: Slc26a9T forms an elongated dimer (~100 Å × 50 Å) with STAS domains protruding 38 Å into the cytosol. The dimer interface is highly unusual, with only 11% of buried surface from transmembrane domain contacts, 16% from STAS-STAS contacts, and the remainder from swapped STAS-TMD interactions. The extended N-terminus binds to the STAS domain and contributes to dimer stability.
evaluation: Claims C56-C61 are directly supported by the cryo-EM structure and quantitative analysis of the dimer interface. The dimensions (C56-C57) are measured from the structure. The unusual nature of the interface (C58) is supported by comparison to other proteins with similar folds. The quantitative breakdown of buried surface areas (C59-C60) is calculated from the structure. The role of the N-terminus (C61) is observed structurally, though functional validation of its contribution to stability could strengthen this claim.

result: The STAS domains act as the primary platform for subunit interactions in the Slc26a9T dimer. The STAS domain structure closely resembles those from SLC26A5 (Prestin) and SLC26Dg, consisting of a six-stranded β-sheet core with four α-helices. Specific loop regions make contacts with the opposing TMD, and these contact residues are strongly conserved among family members. The removed IVS and CT regions would be positioned away from the dimer interface, available for interactions with accessory proteins.
evaluation: Claims C62-C69 are well-supported by the structural data and sequence analysis. The role of STAS domains as interaction platforms (C62) is directly observed and consistent with previous functional studies showing deleterious effects of STAS mutations. The structural similarity to other STAS domains (C63) validates the model. The specific contacts (C65) and their conservation (C66) are observed from the structure and sequence alignments. The inference about the location of removed regions (C69) is reasonable based on the truncated structure.

result: The transmembrane domain (TMD) conforms to a 7+7 inverted repeat topology with 14 membrane-inserted α-helices, segregated into a convex core module (α1-4, 9-11) carrying the ion-binding site and a concave gate module (α5-7, 12-14). The TMD shows high similarity to SLC26Dg (RMSD 2.0 Å). The structure represents an inward-open state, with a large cavity accessible from the intracellular side but no contiguous pore to the extracellular side.
evaluation: Claims C70-C76 are strongly supported by the structural data and comparison to related proteins. The topology (C70-C71) and domain organization (C72-C73) are directly observed in the structure. The similarity to SLC26Dg (C74) with RMSD of 2.0 Å indicates high structural conservation. The identification of an inward-open state (C76) is a reasonable inference from the structural features described in C75, though definitive assignment of conformational states typically benefits from multiple structures or additional functional data.

result: The nanodisc structure differs from the detergent structure in the conformation of the core module, which has rotated approximately 14° and moved 4 Å toward the extracellular side. This conformation likely represents an intermediate state on the transition toward an outward-facing state.
evaluation: Claims C77-C78 are supported by comparison of the two cryo-EM structures. The quantitative description of the conformational change (C77) is measured from the structural superposition. The interpretation as an intermediate state (C78) is a reasonable inference based on the direction and magnitude of the movement, though it remains an interpretation rather than a definitive assignment. The observation of different conformations in different environments strengthens the evidence for an alternate-access mechanism.

result: Slc26a9T has several distinguishing structural features compared to SLC26Dg: a loop-helix structure (α5') that fills a depression at the membrane boundary, an extended extracellular loop between α3-α4 containing predicted glycosylation sites, and a significantly longer N-terminus with scattered helical segments contacting the inner membrane leaflet. These features are likely preserved in mammalian SLC26 transporters due to high sequence conservation.
evaluation: Claims C79-C84 are well-supported by the structural data and sequence analysis. The specific structural features (C79-C83) are directly observed in the cryo-EM structure and clearly distinguished from the bacterial homolog. The prediction of glycosylation sites (C80) is supported by citation to a previous study. The inference that these features are preserved in other mammalian paralogs (C84) is reasonable based on sequence conservation, though direct structural confirmation would strengthen this claim.

result: In the inward-facing conformation, anions enter via a wide aqueous vestibule with positive electrostatic potential from basic residues. The linear I-V relationship of wild-type Slc26a9T is compatible with symmetric rate-limiting barriers. Charge-reversal mutations of basic residues near the binding site (K270E, K443E) cause outward rectification, indicating increased inward barriers, while mutations of extracellular basic residues (K221E, K431E) cause inward rectification.
evaluation: Claims C85-C90 are well-supported by the combination of structural analysis, electrostatic calculations, and mutagenesis data. The structural features and electrostatics (C85) are directly observed. The interpretation of the linear I-V relationship (C86) is supported by citations to previous work on similar systems. The mutagenesis results (C87-C90) provide strong functional validation of the structural observations and electrostatic calculations, demonstrating the importance of these residues for the transport mechanism.

result: An anion binding site is inferred to be located in a pocket of the core domain between the N-termini of α3 and α10, at the apex of the inward-open cavity. This location is equivalent to substrate-binding sites in related transporters. The pocket is smaller than in SLC26Dg due to F128 projecting into it. Residues F128, F92, and L391 contribute to the partly hydrophobic character, while Q88, S392, and T127 could stabilize dehydrated anions.
evaluation: Claims C91-C96 are supported by structural analysis and comparison to related transporters, though the binding site is inferred rather than directly observed (no Cl- density was resolved). The location (C91-C93) is reasonable based on comparison to structures of related transporters where substrate binding has been observed. The structural features of the pocket (C94-C96) are directly observed. However, the specific interactions with anions (C96) remain speculative without direct structural evidence of bound substrate. The subsequent mutagenesis data (C97-C102) provide strong functional support for these inferences.

result: Mutagenesis of binding-site residues alters transport properties: S392A shows inward rectification, F128A and Q88A show outward rectification, while F92A and L391A show minor perturbations. The Q88E mutant shows severely compromised transport. Changes in the permeability-conductivity relationship are most pronounced for S392A and F128A. No binding-site mutants showed major increases in HCO3- or SO42- permeability or evidence of coupled transport.
evaluation: Claims C97-C102 are strongly supported by comprehensive mutagenesis and electrophysiology data. The I-V relationships (C97-C98) and the effects on permeability and conductivity (C100-C101) are directly measured. The severe effect of Q88E (C99) is particularly informative, as it replaces a conserved residue with one found in prokaryotic transporters, providing insight into substrate selectivity. The negative result regarding HCO3- and SO42- permeability in mutants (C102) is important for understanding the determinants of substrate specificity.

result: The dimeric organization of Slc26a9 differs markedly from SLC4 and SLC23 family members, which interact via extended interfaces between gate modules. In Slc26a9, the TMD interface is minimal while subunit interactions are mediated by cytoplasmic STAS domains. Similar minimal TMD contacts were recently proposed for SLC26Dg and observed in the mechanosensitive channel OSCA.
evaluation: Claims C103-C106 are well-supported by structural comparison and citations to previous work. The differences from SLC4 and SLC23 families (C103) are directly observable from structural superposition. The description of the Slc26a9 interface (C104) is supported by the quantitative analysis of buried surface areas. The comparisons to SLC26Dg (C105) and OSCA (C106) appropriately contextualize the findings and show that while unusual, this type of oligomerization is not unprecedented.

result: Slc26a9 shows large uncoupled Cl- currents that saturate at high mM concentrations, properties consistent with a fast bidirectional uniport mechanism rather than a channel. The high Km matches intracellular Cl- concentration, fostering high turnover. Structural data suggest an alternate-access mechanism, with the inward-facing structure showing the binding site accessible to the cytoplasm and the intermediate conformation showing the site buried between core and gate modules. The core module makes ascending/descending rigid-body movements relative to the immobilized gate-STAS complex, resembling an elevator mechanism.
evaluation: Claims C107-C115 are well-supported by the combination of functional and structural data. The functional properties (C107) are confirmed by electrophysiology. The interpretation as a uniport mechanism (C108) is a reasonable inference from the data, though the distinction between a very fast transporter and a channel can be subtle. The structural evidence for an alternate-access mechanism (C111-C114) is strong, with two distinct conformations captured. The comparison to an elevator mechanism (C114-C115) is supported by citations and is consistent with the observed rigid-body movements.

result: Homology to the outward-facing structure of SLC4A1/Band 3 permits anticipation of the extent of conformational changes in Slc26a9, with basic residues likely creating a positive electrostatic environment in the extracellular vestibule. The role of electrostatics is supported by functional experiments and Poisson-Boltzmann calculations. During transport, Cl- is dragged across the transmembrane electric field, likely facilitating conformational changes. A similar mechanism may underlie electromotility in Prestin.
evaluation: Claims C116-C119 are supported by structural homology, electrostatic calculations, and mutagenesis data. The homology modeling (C116) is reasonable given the structural similarity to SLC4A1. The electrostatic calculations (C117) provide quantitative support for the proposed mechanism. The inference about Cl- movement facilitating conformational changes (C118) is reasonable based on the electrostatic properties. The speculation about Prestin (C119) is appropriately tentative and supported by citation, though it remains a hypothesis requiring further testing.

result: The inability of Slc26a9 to transport SO42- is likely related to insufficient binding site interactions for divalent anions, as the site lacks positive countercharges. Other mammalian SLC26 members have similar binding sites but contain a positively charged residue at the position equivalent to V393 in Slc26a9. The inability to transport HCO3- is remarkable given that NO3- is transported; this may be due to perturbation of the HCO3-/CO32- equilibrium at the binding site, with the positive electrostatic potential stabilizing the divalent CO32- form.
evaluation: Claims C120-C124 are supported by structural analysis, homology modeling, and functional data. The explanation for lack of SO42- transport (C120) is a reasonable inference from the binding site structure. The observation about other family members (C121-C122) is supported by sequence alignment and homology modeling. The explanation for lack of HCO3- transport (C123-C124) is more speculative, as it involves a hypothesis about protonation state changes at the binding site that is not directly tested. However, it is a plausible mechanistic explanation consistent with the observed selectivity.

result: High homology between mammalian SLC26 paralogs suggests a common architecture and similar conformational transitions. The diversity of functional phenotypes (uncoupled uniport, coupled exchange, motor activity) could rely on small localized structural differences imposing variable energy barriers. Uncoupled uniporters like Slc26a9 presumably have small barriers permitting unloaded transporter transitions, while coupled exchangers have increased binding affinity and enlarged barriers preventing unloaded transitions. The motor function of Prestin could result from an insurmountable barrier preventing the final transition to an outward-facing state.
evaluation: Claims C125-C130 are largely speculative, though based on reasonable mechanistic principles. The inference about common architecture (C125-C126) is supported by sequence conservation and the structural similarity to SLC26Dg. However, the mechanistic explanations for functional diversity (C127-C130) are hypotheses that, while plausible and consistent with the data, are not directly tested in this study. These claims represent interesting models for future investigation but should be considered speculative interpretations rather than established findings. Direct structural and functional characterization of other family members would be needed to test these hypotheses.

result: Electrophysiology experiments show instantaneous activity not obviously dependent on activating ligands. A potential activation mechanism could be mobilization from intracellular stores, possibly regulated by phosphorylation, consistent with the predominantly intracellular localization of full-length Slc26a9. The IVS may harbor modifiable motif elements involved in surface-trafficking regulation.
evaluation: Claims C131-C133 are speculative regarding regulation mechanisms. The observation of instantaneous activity (C131) is supported by the electrophysiology data. However, the proposed activation mechanisms (C132-C133) are hypotheses based on previous studies and the observed localization differences between full-length and truncated constructs. These are reasonable speculations that warrant further investigation, but they are not directly tested in this study. The authors appropriately note that these hypotheses must be evaluated in more physiologically relevant contexts.

result: SLC26A9 is found in lung and stomach epithelia where it mediates luminal electrogenic chloride transport, contributing to airway clearance and gastric acid production. It colocalizes with CFTR and has proposed regulatory interactions with CFTR. Knockout mice develop airway and gastrointestinal pathologies, and human polymorphisms correlate with altered severity of airway clearance disorders. SLC26A9 has been proposed as a therapeutic target for cystic fibrosis.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C9-C14 summarize established knowledge from previous studies, all supported by appropriate citations. These claims provide important context for the current work but are not novel findings of this study. The citations appear appropriate and the statements accurately represent the current understanding of SLC26A9's physiological roles and therapeutic potential.

result: The SLC26 family consists of ten functional mammalian paralogs with distinct tissue targeting and transport mechanisms. SLC26A5 (Prestin) functions as a voltage-dependent motor protein rather than a transporter. The transport mode of SLC26A9 is controversial, with some reports showing Cl-/HCO3- exchange and others showing uncoupled Cl- conductance. Prior to this study, no high-resolution structures existed for eukaryotic SLC26 members, with structural information limited to the bacterial SLC26Dg. SLC26 transporters form functional oligomers, but the quaternary arrangement was unknown.
evaluation: Claims C15-C26 provide background information about the SLC26 family and the state of knowledge prior to this study. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to previous work. These claims accurately represent the field and establish the rationale for the current structural and functional studies. They are not novel findings but important context.

result: The cryo-EM structures define the general architecture of eukaryotic SLC26 family members and reveal an unusual mode of oligomerization relying predominantly on the STAS domain. The structures support a rapid alternate-access mechanism mediating uncoupled chloride transport with negligible bicarbonate or sulfate permeability. A selective anion binding site is located in the center of a mobile module within the transmembrane domain.
evaluation: Claims C4-C8 represent the major conclusions of the study, stated in the abstract. These are well-supported by the comprehensive structural and functional data presented in the manuscript. The structures (C4) are of sufficient quality to define the architecture. The unusual oligomerization mode (C5) is clearly demonstrated by the quantitative analysis of the dimer interface. The transport mechanism (C6-C7) is supported by both structural evidence (two conformations) and functional data (selectivity, kinetics). The binding site location (C8) is supported by structural analysis and extensive mutagenesis.
